d.title: Six fields you already have, and what each one answers
d.caption: **The event log is an audit trail you did not have to build** — every user message, model response, tool call and state change, ordered and persisted, which is more than most production systems can say about their own decision-making. **And the highest-value observability decision is not a tracing vendor:** it is retaining sessions long enough to investigate complaints. A bad answer reported from last week is answerable in thirty seconds if you still have the events and impossible if you do not. Decide the number, balance it against section 06, and write it down.

d.title: Five cost questions, answerable from two fields
d.caption: **`usage_metadata` on the response event plus `callback_context.agent_name` answers the question every finance conversation about agents eventually reaches:** which part of this system is expensive, and why. d.title: Content capture is a decision about personal data, not a debugging preference
d.caption: **Prompts and responses contain whatever your users typed** — for a support agent that means names, addresses, order details and occasionally a card number somebody pasted in. Capturing full content into a tracing backend copies all of it somewhere with different retention and different access control from your session store, **which may be exactly what your privacy review has not been told about.** `NO_CONTENT` with metadata still tells you which agent, which tool, how many tokens and whether it failed — which answers most operational questions.

d.title: Two metrics, two thresholds, and the asymmetry is deliberate
d.caption: **There is one right sequence of tool calls and many acceptable ways to phrase an answer**, which is exactly what the two thresholds encode: trajectory must match at 1.0, response only has to reach 0.8. **Note what `agent_module` wants** — an importable package exposing `root_agent`, the same layout `adk web` expects, so the thing you evaluate is the thing you run. A directory path runs every case file in it.

d.title: Two contradictory answers scored 0.46
d.caption: **That number is the most important thing in the lesson.** The agent said *“It is 14C and raining in London”* where the reference said *“London is sunny and 25 degrees”*: contradictory answers, nearly half marks, because the metric is ROUGE — it compares n-grams and two sentences sharing “London”, “is” and “and” score well regardless of agreement. **So a high score does not mean the answer is right and a low one does not mean it is wrong.** Use it to catch large regressions; reach for a model-graded metric when correctness is the question.

d.title: num_runs=2 because a model is stochastic - and a flaky case is information
d.caption: **A single run tells you about one sample, so running each case twice distinguishes a regression from sampling noise** — at a cost that multiplies directly, which is the argument for a small set run often rather than a large one run rarely. **The instinct when a case flaps is to loosen the threshold, and sometimes that is right:** a reference phrased too specifically will flap for no reason. But a case that genuinely passes half the time is telling you the agent is unreliable on that input, and the user experience is exactly that coin flip.

d.title: Five things that belong in the set, and one that does not
d.caption: **Fixed bugs are the highest-value cases by a distance:** a user reported it, you fixed it, and now it cannot come back silently. Refusals are the ones most often left out, and a guardrail with no test is a guardrail that stops working when somebody rewrites the instruction. **And the framing to keep:** 85% on your set means the agent handles your twenty cases as well as it did last week. It says nothing about the questions you did not think of, and it is not a number to report as “the agent is 85% accurate”.

d.title: Sixty lines, and the half of the value people skip
d.caption: **Recording the requests lets you assert on what the framework *sent*, which is where most interesting behaviour lives:** did the instruction interpolate state correctly, was the tool declared, did history grow as expected, did `include_contents="none"` really send nothing. **Several measurements in this course came from reading `seen` rather than the output** — including the one showing that a long conversation resends everything. And because it subclasses `BaseLlm`, ADK treats it as a model in every respect: nothing else is stubbed.

d.title: Seven behaviours worth a test, and the index that catches everyone
d.caption: **The script index advances per model call, not per turn:** a turn with one tool call consumes two entries — the response requesting the tool and the response answering it. Give a script too few and later calls fall off the end, which shows up as an agent saying something nonsensical rather than as a clean failure. **When a test behaves strangely, count the model calls first.**

d.title: Fresh lists per fake, and why the suite's speed is the point
d.caption: **`script` and `seen` are class attributes, so a shared mutable default leaks state between tests in a way that is genuinely confusing to debug** — passing fresh lists in the fixture is the whole fix. **And the timing matters as much as the assertions:** a suite finishing in under a second gets run on every save, while one taking two minutes because it calls a real model gets run before a release, which is to say after the mistake has been built on. Speed is what makes a test suite a design tool rather than a gate.
